title: Returning from vacation? The government can search your phone without a warrant.
gist: Immigration advocate Thomas Kennedy sued the federal government to delete data he believes CBP copied from his phone during a ~45-minute seizure at Miami International Airport, alleging he was targeted for his political organizing. CBP relies on the long-recognized Fourth Amendment border exception and says it searched devices of only 55,318 of 419 million travelers in FY2025.

insights.claim: Federal courts have long recognized a border exception to the Fourth Amendment under which people, bags and electronic devices can be searched without a warrant at US ports of entry.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Travelers' devices, including corporate devices carrying sensitive data, have weak legal protection at US borders.
insights.quote: Federal courts have long-recognized a “border exception” to the Fourth Amendment of the US Constitution

insights.claim: CBP says it searched the electronic devices of 55,318 international travelers out of over 419 million processed at ports of entry in fiscal 2025, which the article states as 0.0013% (the arithmetic actually gives about 0.013%).
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Device searches are rare in absolute terms but number in the tens of thousands per year.
insights.quote: CBP only searched the electronic devices of 55,318 international travelers

insights.claim: CBP states it can copy device data if there is probable cause that it contains evidence of a violation of law it enforces, or if the information relates to immigration, customs or other enforcement matters.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: The broad 'relates to immigration' standard gives agents wide discretion to copy data.
insights.quote: if the information relates to immigration, customs, or other enforcement matters.

insights.claim: Thomas Kennedy alleges a CBP agent at Miami International Airport threatened prolonged interrogation and indefinite phone retention unless he surrendered his phone, which was taken away for about 45 minutes before he was released without charges.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Coercive consent tactics are likely to be tested in litigation over device searches.
insights.quote: they could retain my phone indefinitely

insights.claim: Kennedy, who works with the Florida Immigration Coalition, Amnesty International and the Community Justice Project, believes CBP flagged him for his immigrant-rights organizing and is suing to have the copied data deleted.
insights.speaker: Ars Staff
insights.so_what: Claims of viewpoint-based border searches raise civil-liberties and political risk around immigration enforcement.
insights.quote: I believe CBP flagged me because of my organizing and political work around immigrants’ rights in Florida
